speechtext: The house resumed from Tuesday, April 10, consideration in committee of Bill No. 42, respecting relief measures-Mr. Gordon-Mr. Gobeil in the chair.

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OP RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
When the house adjourned last evening the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) was answering an argument which had been
raised earlier in the evening. The suggestion had been made that certain words which appeared in the 1933 act had been omitted from the 1934 bill, namely:
Notwithstanding the provisions of any statute or law the governor in council may,-
(a)	-loan or advance money to or guarantee the payment of money by any public body, corporation or undertaking;
Section 2, subsection (v) of the present bill reads:
Notwithstanding the provisions of any statute or law the governor in council may,-
(b)	When parliament is not in session, to take all such measures as in his discretion may be deemed necessary or advisable to maintain, within the competence of parliament, peace, order and good government throughout Canada;
Then I would emphasize these particular words:
-and at all times to take all such measures as in his discretion may be deemed necessary or advisable to protect and maintain the credit and financial position of the dominion or any province thereof.
I submit that these words, broad in their meaning, can give to the governor in council the power to guarantee payments in the same way as the guarantee was given to the Canadian Pacific Railway last year, and as evidence of that I suggest that we should look at the order in council, prepared by the Prime Minister himself, granting the guarantee to the Canadian Pacific. First I would ask hon. members to observe the wording of clause (b) of section 2, especially the words I have just quoted, and compare them with the language of clause 9 of the order in council as drafted by the Prime Minister, reading as follows:
That the said railway company is a public corporation carrying on its operations not only in Canada but in other parts of the world; and, in the opinion of the ministers, under present disturbed economic conditions, it is desirable to prevent default by the said railway company in discharging its said capital obligations and indebtedness as they mature, and in the public interest, to grant the request of the said railway company as a measure for the protection and maintenance of the credit and financial position of Canada.
I ask the committee to note the similarity between the wording of clause (b) of the present section we are considering and the basis of the guarantee as drafted in the order in council. The Prime Minister repeated, in his evidence before the banking and commerce committee, that he gave the guarantee because he believed it to be in the national interest, and he said further, " What I then did I would do to-morrow." I submit that under this section as we now have it he could
Relief Act, 1934

do the very thing he did in granting the guarantee to the Canadian Pacific Railway. He said further that there cannot be any opinion as to an act of parliament.

Relief Act, 1934

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OP RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
Those items refer to
something that should not now be discussed before the committee. We are at present dealing with 1934 legislation. The 1930 legislation and the disbursements under it were discussed in 1931, and just why the time of parliament should now be taken up except for an obvious purpose for discussing the expenditure in 1930 is something I am sure the hon. member will be able to answer to his constituents. The appropriation was made in 1930 to the grade crossing fund and the next year a similar sum was appropriated. Those who are familiar with the operation of that fund will realize that there is still a deficiency in it; in fact it would require a very substantial sum of money to make good the amount needed to meet the demands upon the fund under legislation passed by parliament in previous years. There are pending before the board of railway commissioners applications for a very large number of grade crossings. I thought my memory was good enough to state the number, but I cannot do so at the moment. It is not improbable that something will have to be done to add to that fund this year. For instance, in Hamilton just before the advent to power of this government, certain recommendations with respect to level crossings were made and later the then Minister of Labour, the late Senator Robertson, after conferences with the city and the railway authorities, undertook that certain grade crossings would be assisted, and they have been completed, but the money that is payable to the city and the railway company under the provisions of the agreement has not yet been paid. This matter covered some of the payments that were made under the direction of the board of railway commissioners.

speechtext:
There is a matter that I
would like to draw to the attention of the government and that I hope will receive consideration when funds being provided by this legislation are being disbursed. I have already on more than one occasion indicated the situation that prevails in one part of my constituency and extending also into that of the hon. member for Souris. I would likewise like to direct attention to a resolution that came into my hands this morning and that was passed at a meeting of the reeves of four municipalities, as follows:
At a meeting of the reeves of the municipalities of Pembina, Louise, Roblin and Turtle Mountain, held at Killarney on the 6th day of 74726-129
April, 1934, it was resolved that we hereby request the government of the province of Manitoba to petition the federal government to give the same consideration to these municipalities in regard to the payment of freight charges on feed, fodder and seed as that given to the area known as Manitoba drought area "A" as given by privy council order No. 2384.
I would like to say a word in regard to this particular area. Those who are familiar with the situation will know that in the extreme southwestern part of Manitoba there is a large area that has suffered very severely from drought. The area of which I speak is not nearly so extensive but at the same time it is one that has suffered severely and from neither the provincial nor the federal government has assistance come to which I think that particular section is entitled. Because the area is somewhat smaller it was excluded from the arrangements that were made between the two governments in regard to the extreme southwest of the province. But this area of which I speak suffered very severely, not only last year but for two or three preceding years. As regards one part of this area, perhaps the Prime Minister will remember that I called it to his attention a year or two ago when I requested that the customs charges on the importation of feed should be reduced.

This area, not only the Pembina district, but further west, Louise, Robin, ATgyle, has suffered very severely. I had occasion to call attention to that fact twice when I mentioned the great disaster that overtook them because of the mortality among their horses. I

think I mentioned that sixty-nine, as I am credibly informed, had died in one township. All that this resolution asks is that consideration should be given to the question of freight charges which were reduced to the benefit of the area further west. In the letter accompanying the resolution the writer indicates that they have the assurance that the provincial government will make such an application. I would like to have an assurance that if the provincial government makes that application, the federal government will deal with it in the same way as it dealt with what is referred to as drought area " A " in southwestern Manitoba. (Last fall I took pains to drive through all this district and I found conditions there deplorable indeed, and if there is any section of the country that is entitled to whatever assistance can be given by either this or the provincial government, I shall be only too happy to press its case with all the vigour I can.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OP RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
The hon. member for Lisgar is of course aware of the fact that each succeeding year representatives of the provincial authorities have presented to the federal government claims for consideration, and those have been sometimes for the payment of freight, of feed, sometimes to move cattle from one area to another, sometimes to pay freight charges for the transport of household effects and the family itself from the south to the north; but in every case it has been a matter of discussion and consideration between the federal and provincial authorities. As the matter stands now, until this legislation is enacted no agreements of any kind can be made between the provinces and the dominion. Several matters such as that to which the hon. member refers are being pressed upon the minister from Saskatchewan and one or two from Alberta. What the hon. member has said with respect to the southwestern section of Manitoba is known to the government, not only by reason of the representations made in the house by himself and others, but also by reason of the fact that the department's communications with the provincial government have pointed out the crop failures in that particular section, which in a previous year, but not last year, if my memory serves me aright, extended, as the hon. gentleman knows, far into Saskatchewan. Last year I think there was a crop in the Saskatchewan area, but not in that area in Manitoba, to which he refers. All these matters, I assure the hon. gentleman, will receive the most careful consideration of the minister and the government if thev have

any authority to deal with them. Until this statute passes they have no such authority, either to grant assistance or to refuse; they can merely advise, as I have been doing, that until the legislation is enacted they have no power to enter into any agreement.

women and children receiving relief in that area, an almost incredibly large number of people to be receiving relief in that particular area. Our advances to enable the province to function, as distinguished from loans, include that $22,000,000. I fancy the hon. gentleman has seen the orders in council, because they were tabled here during the years in which the expenditures were made.

speechtext: What I want to get clear is whether or not all the money spent by the relief commission in area A, that is the area in which the commission took full charge of the relief, was furnished by the federal government, and if any of it is being collected from the province.

It was stated in this chamber, with the unanimous approval of the house, that this was a national calamity in regard to which the central power should assume responsibility for the entire expenditures.
The other amount consists of items that represent our proportion of expenditures under the agreements made with Saskatchewan. Do I make myself clear?

speechtext:
Mention of the Saskatchewan relief commission brings up a problem which has been very widely discussed in the eastern portion of Alberta, where the people feel they have a very great grievance. As the Prime Minister knows, the constituency of Medicine Hat runs adjacent to the Saskatchewan boundary for two hundred miles. To the east of the boundary relief is administered by a commission, who send men to the various districts and who seem to hand out relief in a sympathetic and almost a generous manner. This is done, of course, because the people in that section have suffered four successive crop failures largely due to the dry winds and drought. But these dry winds do not stop at the interprovincial boundary line; year after year they have also destroyed the crops on the Alberta side of the boundary. In Alberta relief is administered in a very different way. People found that not only were their crops destroyed but their garden crops were failures as well. Some of those who had trucks went to the neighbouring irrigation districts and brought back large loads of fresh vegetables which they distributed free of charge to the people. People in other provinces also generously supplied fresh vegetables to these districts free of cost, and that was greatly appreciated. The people in those districts, however, find difficulty in getting ordinary relief. In that whole strip of country, which is thirty miles wide, there are only two police officers. The people do not have automobiles; they must walk or drive their horses twelve or fifteen miles to find a police officer, and often when they get there he is not at home. Then the officer has to go back with them and investigate the case, and sometimes these officers are hard boiled. If they see chickens or cattle on the farm they feel that

Relief Act, 1934
the man is not destitute and should not get relief. So these people feel they have a grievance, because just across the boundary they see relief administered in a more generous manner.
The merchants of the district also have a complaint. They get very few relief orders. I was talking to a merchant in the Saskatchewan area who said he had two hundred customers, of whom one hundred and ten bring in relief orders, so the people there are thoroughly convinced that there is discrimination in respect to relief as between the two provinces. As the Prime Minister has said, the dominion does not expect to get any money back; usually the province does not expect to get money back, but we find that the municipalities and the improvement districts are trying to get these people to work for their relief. No one objects very much to that, but what relief is given is deducted from the allowances in the improvement districts. I know that this is largely a provincial matter, but according to my information the province has applied to have a relief commission for the eastern part of Alberta, and I hope to convince the minister of the necessity of reviewing the situation in this district.

Mr. Chairman, the observations made by the Prime Minister with regard to the division of authority as between the provincial and federal governments impels me to say what I had intended to say at some other time. It seems to me that all the efforts in connection with relief in the last few years, and as contemplated under the bill now before the committee, have been predicated upon the assumption that this is an emergency only. I should like to venture the opinion that while relieving the distress of the unemployed is an emergency in an aggravated form, unemployment has become and will continue to be a more or less permanent factor. One would hope that as the years go by and as we return to a condition of normalcy, as one statesman of the United States called it, there would not be as great a degree of unemployment; that perhaps through the sharing of work, and for other reasons, nearly everybody will have employment. I believe, however, that for some years to come there will continue to be what one might term an irreducible minimum of unemployment, and that that has to be dealt with.
The point I wish to make is this, that if the government has not yet taken any steps in the matter it might very well now, either by the appointment of a commission, or of themselves, make investigations looking to the solution of the problem of providing for the permanently unemployed. The government itself and all hon. members in the house, regardless of their political affiliations,
Relief Act, 1934

have expressed themselves as being in favour of a form of unemployment insurance. I believe it was two sessions ago the Prime Minister said that unemployment insurance was a very difficult matter with which to deal, and that a good deal of time would be required to ascertain all the implications of unemployment insurance. He believed investigations would need to be made so that any legislation brought in would operate properly, under certain actuarial conditions, and so forth. But it seems to me that if the government could see its way clear to appoint a commission, if you like-and one hesitates to advocate the appointment of a commission, because there seems to be a great deal of public antagonism towards the adoption of such a course-it might consider the question from this point of view, namely, that nearly all these social problems ought, in a sense, to be coordinated under one federal control or, at least, under some sort of reasonable system. It might become possible that with unemployment insurance legislation there could be coordinated such things as workmen's compensation, widows' allowances, insurance for ill health, old age pensions, and poor relief. Then, combined with the investigations info the possibility of coordinating these services under federal control, there would of course arise the necessity of dealing with the provinces, because I appreciate that in this connection there is the question of invading their jurisdiction. The Prime Minister has spoken about the difficulty presented by the fact that the provinces are in control of some of these activities. I rise only to say that the government would do well to consider this suggestion, because in the future time might be saved if they at once appointed a commission for the purpose of investigating these matters. There would be many other features besides the ones I have mentioned. For instance, the commission could report to the government as to what form the unemployment insurance should take, whether it should be contributory or non-contributory -although the government is already on record in that connection-as to the proportion which should be paid by employer and empIo3ree; as to the proportion which should be paid by federal, provincial and municipal governments, and where the money should come from to make the payments-bv special tax, or some other method. I am making these references in a more or less indirect way, and have not been particularly definite.
I believe, however, there is merit in the suggestion that the government might now take steps to make these investigations so that at

the earliest possible moment a definite scientific system, if we may call it that, could be evolved and enacted into law at the earliest possible moment.

speechtext:
The question of social
services to be rendered to the people of a country by its government is one which has engaged the attention of peoples for nearly half a century. The burden placed upon governments has increased so greatly that the taxation necessarily imposed to meet the demands is, in some of the provinces, nearly as great as was their whole taxation at the time they came into being. Mothers' allowances, health insurance and old age pensions -and then, of course, there is the Workmen's Compensation Act, which I had intended to deal with separately, because it is more than a social service-all these are administered by the provinces. It will be recalled that the Workmen's Compensation Act is the embodiment of a principle, which principle is that an assessment must be made against industry for the purpose of providing a fund to meet the damage effected by industry to those employed in it. I have used the word "damage" rather than any other word, because actions which used to be taken in the courts were taken to recover damages for injuries. This act provides that a fixed sum shall be taken from industry every month for the purpose of creating a fund to satisfy the claims of those employed in the industry of a particular province. The consumer pays that tax.
Secondly, health insurance, which is part of the modern social insurance of Great Britain and on the continent of Europe, involves the payment of a sum based upon actuarial computations as to the period of illnesses of individuals, to enable a fixed sum per week to be paid, after a given period of illness, to those who are employed in industry. That is largely paid by the consumer. Now we come to old age pensions, and we find that in this country it is paid seventy-five per cent by the federal power and twenty-five per cent by the provincial power, that it is a sum payable to those who have reached the age of seventy years, and that it is paid to the extent of 820 per month. Those payments are made by the consumers, in the form of taxation. Then, lastly, there are mothers' benefits, or benefits which are created by statute to enable those who are deprived of the assistance of their husbands to maintain their children and enable them to give-and I shall use very broad terms-such training as will be sufficient to fit the children for

Relief Act, 1934
life's struggles. That also is paid by the provinces and involves an obligation being placed upon the taxpayers.	_
Those are forms of benefit which are paid directly or indirectly by the state to those engaged in industry, to those who have attained a given age or to others who have been deprived of a breadwinner. Then, of course, there is the ordinary, normal relief, which is an obligation placed upon the provinces, and in turn upon the municipalities. In the budgets of every province one could find year after year, long before the years 1929 or 1930, provision for indigents or for the poor, administered-and I am looking at the hon. member for Vancouver Centre-in remote communities such as those in British Columbia, where municipal institutions had not been set up, by the gold commissioner, and administered in the older provinces by municipal councils. This is indigent relief, or poor relief.
There were in this dominion before the depression set in an average of 143,000 people who had to be cared for, during the period they were unable to work, either by the savings they had made or by contributions made by the taxpayers. The hon. member for North Waterloo has pointed out that the number is now much larger. Undoubtedly it is much larger, not solely because of the depression but because of circumstances to which the hon. member for Wetaskiwin referred only the other day. This is the age of machinery; four men are now doing the work that seven did in 1920. The result is that you have to seek employment for that surplus population. For instance, take the everyday business of life which any one of us can recall from the days when we were ten years of age. We see year after year a lessening of the number employed in providing services for our comfort, for our convenience, and shall we say for our pleasure as well.
The hon. gentleman should keep in mind the fact that during all the period through which we have passed an effort has been made to collect such information as would enable us to have a picture of the situation, and we have that picture in a fairly complete way. It will be recalled that in the census we set up special inquiries for the purpose of giving us some idea of what was the situation throughout Canada. We have the reports of trades unions, and we have the reports of the establishments of industry giving us the number of people employed, the capacity for employment, and the extent
to which that capacity has been taken up during the months which have passed. I say with all deference to the committee that that is a fairly simple thing. It requires patience and time and effort, but there is no difficulty in getting it if you take the time and have the patience to do it. That information has been fairly well secured in this country and we have it in fair shape.
However, when you come to deal with the problem of the creation of facilities to meet that situation you are confronted at once with divided jurisdiction. The provinces have exclusive legislative control over the matters mentioned in section 92 of the British North America Act. Unless there is agreement by them all, you will have a situation such as you have to-day with respect to old age pensions.

If I have the jurisdiction, I need nothing further in the way of information. I say that very frankly because we have spent enormous effort and considerable time and patience to see that that is available. All I can usefully say to this committee is that I hold a very strong opinion as to the necessity of an early revision of the provisions of the British North America Act. I am not unmindful of the fact, and I trust the committee will always keep this in mind, that sometimes there is an inclination on the part of many of us to be intolerant because of the views expressed by those who do not agree with us as to the desirability or necessity of amending that statute. I should like to remind the committee of what I am sure is in its mind always, that the British North America Act represents a compromise, and compromises are always difficult to change without the consent of all those whose interests may be affected. Every member
Relief Act, 1934

of this committee recognizes that difficulty. I need not go into it at any length, beyond stating that we recognize the difficulty and any steps we may take towards its solution will be taken in such a way as not to strain the mechanism of our existing machinery. When we have accomplished that we will be enabled to embark upon those improvements in our legislation which the circumstances clearly necessitate.
My attention has been directed to the fact that I said that before the depression period there were 143,000 who had to be taken care of, but I might state that that number does not include dependents. If we reckoned the way we do now, the number would be somewhere in excess of 400,000. The information given to me by those who make it their business to study this matter and report upon it as carefully as possible is that 143,000 would be an underestimate. I should have indicated that the 143,000 included only earners and not their dependents.
I am grateful to the hon. member for bringing up this matter, but it is clearly not a matter which we should endeavour to discuss under this measure. I have before me the recommendations which the provinces arrived at with the dominion last spring. I say very frankly to the committee that I had hoped we might be able to dispense with a relief measure this year. At the meeting in January the provinces indicated their views in these words:
That until such time as the large numbers of unemployed throughout Canada have been substantially absorbed, either by improved industrial employment or by federal works, federal assistance to the provinces should be continued on the basis of the provinces dealing with present economic conditions by the distribution of direct relief as provided in the existing agreement between the dominion and the provinces.
That is the conclusion at which the provinces arrived. I have explained how we dealt with these matters. At the conference we stated what the situation was, and each premier made a statement as to the situation in his province. They then retired for the purpose of considering how they could best deal with the difficulties which confronted them, and that is the recommendation they made. It was unanimous, but they expressed the hope, in common with ourselves, that conditions would obviate the expenditure of large sums for relief.
I should like the committee to know that there is a very distinct improvement in this country. I will admit that in the country west of the great lakes it is less apparent than

it is in the east. Shorn of their great reservoir of earnings by reason of a lack of profits, the millions of dollars which are normally available for business are no longer available. That means a diminution of purchasing power, and until there is an improvement in agriculture, in prices and otherwise, it is quite apparent that the general improvement must be delayed. However, in the camps maintained by the Department of National Defence where, as I explained yesterday, the men may leave to take positions in agriculture, industry or otherwise, the number has diminished by substantially 9,000. One industry has reported that during February it had the largest production of any month in its history, and it has been in existence almost since confederation. The same thing has happened in connection with another business. Another significant and striking fact, and one which fills us with the spirit of hope and optimism, is the increase in the production of electrical energy. I always regard these figures as an important factor, electrical energy being used to the extent it is in almost every form of industrial activity in Canada. More kilowatts of electrical energy were produced in February than in any month in the history of Canada.

The agreement was made between the railway company and the Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation. The memorandum of the Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation is as follows:
The action taken by the federal government in aid of the imperilled coal and steel industries of Nova Scotia during recent years has included transportation subventions linking up rail and water movements in the navigation season; assisted rail movement in the winter; encouragement to the use of Canadian coal in coke ovens; both in regard to metallurgical coke and domestic coke supplanting imported anthracite; and release of orders for steel rails as an unemployment measure.
The results of this coordinated action of the government have been more stimulating and beneficial than the most optimistic anticipation. The steel plant in Sydney, because of the backlog to its operations given by a 50,000-ton rail order given in the spring of 1933, has been enabled to quote successfully on two rail orders from South Africa, and to obtain substantial orders for export to Great Britain of wire nails, rods and billets.
The direct result of the rail order has been to enable the Sydney steel plant to work on a 50 per cent basis over a period that it is hoped may extend into the summer of 1934. The activity of the steel plant thus made possible has required greater coal consumption, and is on the eve of being reflected in ore and limestone production in Newfoundland, thereby favourably affecting Canadian exports of a general nature to Newfoundland by increasing the purchasing ability of the island. The wisdom of the action of the government taken in aid of the distressed coal mining industry of Nova Scotia has been equally demonstrated by the results in increasing employment.
Coal mining is the life of Nova Scotia. One-quarter of its population, as actual workers, or as the dependants of workers, obtain their livelihood within the province through the mining and transportation of coal, through supplying of mine materials, and in the allied steel industry which is built upon local coal supply. There are other numerous workers beyond the boundaries of Nova Scotia whose livelihood is gained by the handling and distribution of Nova Scotia coal; the benefits of Nova Scotia coal mining in respect to employment being felt throughout all eastern Canada.
A substantial part of the provincial revenue comes from coal royalties.

Relief Act, 1934
Then after discussing the assistance given by coal subventions, he proceeds:
Side by side with this condition in Nova Scotia, coal of non-Canadian origin-the employment from its production benefiting other countries-was being imported into eastern Canada to the extent of 8,000,000 tons of bituminous quality annually, identical in its uses and grade with Nova Scotia coal.
The cost of production of coal in Nova Scotia was increased to a crippling extent by operation of mines at less than half normal rate. The competitive ability of Nova Scotia coal was becoming smaller all the time as the financial resources of employers and workers became exhausted.
The existence of the coal mining industry, which is almost the same thing as the commercial and industrial health of Nova Scotia, was gravely imperilled.
In these imperative circumstances the granting of transportation subventions enabling Canadians to use Nova Scotia coal instead of imported coal was no less than the plain duty of the federal government. As a result coal mining in Nova Scotia has been kept in being, and the use of Nova Scotia coal has been extended to areas formerly exclusively supplied by imported coal, where it has proved to be at least as good quality and as suitable for all kind's of purposes as imported bituminous coal.
The expenditure on subventions has avoided much greater expenditure in necessary workers' relief, has averted calamitous commercial collapse of employing corporations and bankruptcy of municipalities. The assistance given has necessarily been proportionate to the need. The scheme of the coal subventions has in mind the lessening of expenditures as business recovery proceeds. The assistance so far given, based on a need that it is hoped is lessening, has certainly averted conditions requiring such great assistance as to be beyond the powers of government.
Taking all the attendant circumstances into consideration, the action of the government in encouraging the use of Canadian coal by Canadian consumers was plain common sense and has been abundantly justified by what it has accomplished.
I read the whole of that because it covers both the question of subventions in regard to coal and the order for rails.

speechtext:
Perhaps the hon. gentleman is aware that the Soo mill manufactures rails, and has supplied rails in large quantities to the Michigan Central and other American roads operating in Canada as well as to the Canadian Pacific and Canadian National. As a large number of persons were unemployed at the Soo, an order was sought from the railway company. If the railway company required rails they thought they should have

part of the order. The government was then asked whether if the railway company ordered rails the government would give a guarantee to enable operations to be carried on. I suppose it is within the knowledge of this committee that the Algoma Steel Company was in the hands of receivers. Therefore the assistance which I have mentioned was sought. The letter which was written to the minister states:
Our rail mill started on the 30,000 ton unemployment order December 4th and has been operating on single turn in order to distribute the work as much as possible. The order is about one-half rolled and will run to the first week in March.
The operation of the rail mill on this unemployment order has not only restored employment to rail mill employees but has enabled us to secure orders for other material to operate the two merchant mills through the winter. We now have approximately 1,600 men employed, and a payroll of $150,000 per month.
During last summer we had in Sault Ste. Marie over 1,500 families on relief and this would have been increased materially this winter had it not been for the steel plant operation.
That letter is dated January 26, 1934. It is from one of the receivers, the operating receiver.
That is a case in which an arrangement was made between the railway company and the rolling mill, and the rails that were supplied will be taken possession of and paid for as required. I think some of them have been recently shipped into service. The guarantee was given because the company, being in the hands of receivers, could not secure the necessary capital without having some assurance that these rails would be paid for.

The Algoma Steel mill at Sault Ste. Marie had not been operated except part time for probably the past three or four years; I think during the years 1932 and 1933 not more than three

Relief Act, 1934
months. They had a considerable quantity of raw material, iron ore and coal and limestone, as outlined in the order in council. As stated by the Prime Minister, they were in the hands of receivers. The bank was not anxious to advance money to enable this raw material to be manufactured into steel rails, and so the government were approached. As a matter of fact they were approached by representatives of the city of Sault Ste. Marie, not by the company. They were asked if they would guarantee a sufficient portion of the cost of manufacturing these rails to take care of the wages of the men and the cost of such raw material as it might be necessary to purchase. It was done as an unemployment relief proposition entirely. Sault Ste. Marie, as my hon. friend probably knows, has a population of about 23,000 or 24,000 people, 75 per cent of whom are dependent, either directly or indirectly, on the operation of that steel mill for their living. Over 2,000 men are ordinarily employed in the mill. The great majority of these men have been living there for many years. Many of them had their own homes, some of them not entirely paid for. As a result of the mill not operating at all steadily during the past few years these men were unable to find work, unable to provide for their families, and many of them were on relief. As stated in the letter from Mr. Franz, there were some 1,552 families receiving direct relief in the Soo last summer. It was stated by the relief committee, as well as by the mayor, that that number would be undoubtedly increased to much over 2,000 families unless work were provided. After the arrangement was made and the mill put in operation about three months employment was given in the rolling of the rails and approximately another month in getting the mills in shape for operation. This meant about four months of operation, at about $150,000 per month in wages. In other words at least $500,000 was distributed in wages as a result of the order, and instead of there being 1,552 families on relief, as there were last summer, the number fell to something like 640. The saving in direct relief, estimating 1,000 families for four months at $25 per month per family, would be about $100,000. Even if the government had to pay the interest on this guarantee for a period of three years it would not amount to as much as the saving in relief, but I do not expect that the government will have to pay interest for anything like that period of time because, as the Prime Minister has stated, already delivery has been taken of a portion
of the rails. When the Canadian National take delivery they pay for the rails; the money is deposited in the bank and to that extent the guarantee of the government is reduced.

speechtext: I have been given to understand lately that, because of the pooling arrangements that have been made, a great many railway lines are being given up. If I did not misunderstand the statement made by Judge Fullerton only a few days ago, on some of these lines the pooling will be permanent, so I suppose eventually the rails in use will be torn up. I am therefore asking myself the reason for the urgent need of rolling more rails at this particular time and particularly of charging the Canadian National with them, when in some districts, such as my own, the Canadian National rails are being abandoned altogether. According to my recollection of the deliberations of the railway committee for the past few years, these rails are good; in fact they are practically new. I stand to be corrected, but it seems to me that on several occasions the late Sir Henry Thornton stated that one of his great problems was to replace the sixty pound rails with rails weighing eighty pounds and up to one hundred pounds, but that he had carried out that replacement to a considerable extent throughout Canada, and in fact the operation was almost complete. If that were so I fail to see, with all due respect to my hon. friend from West Algoma, and without in any way criticizing him for having endeavoured to do his best to provide employment for the unemployed in his constituency by reopening a mill which had been abandoned for three or four years-

Well, a mill which had been in the hands of a receiver and had not been operating for three or four years. I rather fail to see the justification for the govern-
Relief Act, 193i

ment guaranteeing a transaction such as this and forcing the rails on the Canadian National, which, as I remember it from last year, was to be kept entirely free from political influence, either sectional or local. That was why we appointed all these trustees. I remember at that time pointing out to the members of this house that the difficulty under which the Canadian National had laboured in the past had not been due to petty political pressure but had been due to large demands from large sections or provinces, and that there was nothing to prevent the Canadian National trustees from submitting to such sectional pressure, that nothing in the act we passed last year could bring about that result. Of course I was told that the views I then expressed were altogether without foundation, but now we find that we have unloaded on the Canadian National fifty thousand tons of rails from Nova Scotia and thirty thousand tons of rails from the Algoma Steel Company. I fail to see what justification exists for these orders in council from the standpoint of looking after our greatest problem, namely the Canadian National Railways, and I should be glad to have that explained to me.

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OP RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
Coming from the city of Sydney and having a fairly intimate knowledge of this transaction I want to say that nothing this government has done can be justified quite as easily as the action taken in this connection. There is no doubt at all, as every person who uses the Canadian National knows, that rails must be replaced. There is need of replacements in the eastern section now, and it was simply a matter of justice and good business for this government to agree to guarantee the payment to the banks of the money which was advanced to supply those rails. The effect of these orders has been to transport a large section of the industrial east from the depths of despair to a fair measure of prosperity at the present time. The steel company at Sydney was not operating; true, the fires had not been put out but it was just lingering on. Delegations not only from the steel company but composed of representative men from all parts of the county of Cape Breton came here and laid their case before the government, showing them that the rails were needed and what would be the effect of such an order. The result, so far as the city of Sydney is concerned, where we had fifty per cent of the people on relief, was to take at least seventy per cent of those people off relief, and these rail orders have also affected the production of coal, with the result that

to-day our mines in Cape Breton are being operated to a greater extent, considering the time of year, than has been the case during the past ten years. The steel company is employing perhaps seventy per cent of the men it formerly employed, and in the city of Sydney relief distribution has fallen to perhaps twenty-five or thirty per cent of what it was three years ago. I would suggest to hon. gentlemen opposite that when they discuss a matter such as this they do so having in mind the Canadian point of view.

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OP RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext: The Canadian National point of view.

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OP RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext: Simply because these rails come from one or two parts of Canada is no indication that there is not equally as great an effect upon the western portion of our country. This is one country, and the lines separating the provinces are purely imaginary. If the province of Alberta prospers, the province of Nova Scotia prospers, and vice versa. I have no desire to criticize the managements of the Canadian National Railways who held office in days gone by. It is true, as one railway man has said, that they spent money like drunken sailors. We are now suffering for it. But if the fact remains that the Canadian National Railways must in a certain number of years have their rails relaid I say that the mills in Canada should be allowed to furnish them. Because of this increased work relief which would otherwise be necessary is rendered unnecessary.

dealing with them this afternoon. To assert that we were endeavouring to force rails upon the Canadian National Railways is, in my judgment, rather-shall I say-insulting to the intelligence of the committee.

I shall not reply to the hon. member in kind; I think perhaps he can deal with his own condition. But I do desire to say this, that the trustees were not appointed until January of this year, and that these transactions were those of last year. The transaction supplying rails to the Canadian National Railways was one carried on between the railway company and the mills. But the mills could not carry on, so far as the financial position was concerned, without assistance from the government in the manner indicated. To suggest that this government was endeavouring to force the Canadian National Railways to buy rails at the "Soo" when it has already put into track something like 2,500 tons of them is not, I suggest, quite what should be said with respect to a matter of this kind. Everyone who is familiar with modem railroading knows that the heavy engines used on both railroads in Canada have necessitated the relaying of track. The old 60-pound steel has been changed not only to 80-pound, but to 105-pound sections. And the old 56-pound rail, which was laid on the Canadian Pacific railway when I went west, was a rail produced by Krupps in Germany and by the Barrow firm. I believe there is not now between Vancouver and Montreal a single rail on the main line which does not bear the name of a Canadian mill. Of course on the American end of the Canadian National Railways' line to Chicago, Canadian rails are not laid. Heavy rails put in place in consequence of heavy motive power have cost a great deal of money, and the lighter weight rails have been taken out of track and put into branch lines.
I understand-and I want to be very careful about this because I am not definitely informed-but I understand that the 2,500 tons of rails which have already left the "Soo" have been put in the London section of the Canadian National Railways which, as the hon. gentleman knows, is on the main line to Chicago, a line on which heavy motive power has been used necessitating a rail section much heavier than the old rails before used. I do assure the committee that no effort was made to induce the Canadian National Railways, as a matter of politics or otherwise, to order rails they did not want.
The answer is that if in March of 1934, 2,500 tons had been taken out for the purpose of placing in tracks, one will readily realize that the rails were needed. For instance, to my knowledge, from a statement made by one of the officials, the "Soo" mills are now continuing to roll rails for the Canadian Pacific Railway, which also requires replacements. Those who are familiar with the strain upon rails brought about by modern highspeed trains, and the efforts which have been made to secure rails which will withstand the tremendous pressure of high speed and heavy loads, will know that the railway companies are always, shall I say hungry, for new rails. The only question is that of holding them down, so far as possible from spending unnecessarily in rail purchases.
If there is anything in this transaction which should not have been done I should like to know what it is. I was here when at least one contract was completed, and I know of nothing that any business man would not have done. As a matter of fact the transaction saved money. To be perfectly frank about it, that is the fact: It saved us money. In other words the interest we pay was less than the sum we would have been obligated to pay under direct relief measures for the community in question. The prices paid for rails were the standard prices prevailing at that time. I think that if the hon. gentleman will take the trouble to look up rail prices he will find there was no addition to the ordinary prices for rails of a similar type.

Perhaps the difficulty of the hon. gentleman can be explained. He has not allowed for the fact that the rolling mills were not in a position financially to carry a loan from the banks until such time as delivery was to be made. In other words, the delivery was enlarged far beyond the period of time that it is usual for the purpose of getting money. I do not think it is necessary to go into the financial position of the companies. One of them was in the hands of receivers and the banks had advanced all that they cared to advance. I suggested that they might get a further advance on receivers' certificates but that was found not to be practicable. The order in council was passed in the form in which it is because the advances made by the banks were quite substantial and they were thus able to know that the money advanced for wages would be repaid.
The hon. gentleman has referred to the fact that the ore was purchased in a foreign country. The fact is that there was on hand a substantial quantity of ore, limestone, and the other commodities which go into the production of steel. This applied both to the company at Sault Ste. Marie and the one at Sydney, although the position at Sydney was not perhaps just the same as at Sault Ste. Marie. I do not think I am discussing the private business of the company when I say that the banks felt that under the then existing economic conditions they had advanced all the money that they should advance. If they were going to make payments against the production of rails which would not be paid for immediately, during the time between the completion of production and the time the rails were taken by the purchasers to put on the track they would find themselves with substantial moneys locked up under conditions with which they did not care to deal. Hence it is that this arrangement was made.
As far as the forcing of rails on the Canadian National Railways is concerned, I appeal to any hon. gentleman who has sat on the committee to state if he has not found that the difficulty is to prevent rails being required by the railway. The flattening out of rails by the heavy high speed steel trains and motive power has necessitated the laying of new rails, and all members who have sat on the select committee-I observe one of them in front of me now-will realize that what I say is correct. The general manager and president of the railway has always stated that he is compelled to put in heavy rails,

The reason this guarantee was given was the lapse of time between the date of the completion of the order and the uncertainty as to when the railway company would take possession of the rails to put them on the track. They required financial assistance and it was given to them in this manner.

The financial assistance was not really necessary in order to permit them to begin operations. From the statement if the Prime Minister I understand that botu companies had large quantities of raw materials on hand. With an order in their possession and large stocks of raw materials on hand there would be a strong argument against the necessity of a guarantee. I have sat on the special committee ever since it has been inaugurated-I sat on that committee even before the right hon. gentleman came into the house-and I know as well as the Prime Minister that there has always been a demand for rails. But I know also that there has been a preaching in this house and throughout the country day in and day out for the cutting to the bone of expenditures on the Canadian National Railways. I know also that lines are being abandoned right and left, trains are being pooled, and men are being thrown out of work. We are told we must not put too much pressure on the Canadian National Railways, and it seems incomprehensible that we should order rails in advance. As the Prime Minister has pointed out, the government is to pay interest during the time which elapses from the completion of the contract and the time the rails are taken by the company. In one order in council arrangement is made for the payment of $13,000 in interest and in the other there is an arrangement between the corporation and the bank. Order in council, P.C. 1285, which deals with the Algoma Steel Corporation, reads:
That the corporation and the said bank will give to the dominion government such assurances as may be requisite to provide that fifty per cent of the rails manufactured under the terms of this proposal shall be earmarked and held as security against advances made under the dominion's guarantee to the bank and upon payment being made for the said rails by the railway company, in whole or in part, the money paid therefor to the bank by the railway company shall effectually release the dominion government from the guarantee to the extent of such payment.
So that there was a kind of joint arrangement there, as I understand it. I do not intend to proceed very much further with the matter; I simply want to make myself clear.
I think I am within my rights in inquiring into the reasons which brought about the guaranteeing of such large sums to the banks, who have been stating in the public press and elsewhere that they had any amount of money to lend to good borrowers, and I know of no better borrower than a man who has a government order in his pocket; I have never heard of any better borrower anywhere throughout the country. It has been almost an axiom that a person who had an order from the government could go to any bank and, by transferring the order, obtain the money to carry it out.

I did not in any sense object to furnishing such information as the government had, but I did say to the hon. gentleman, and I think he must have heard me, that the government had no information as to the extent to which the rails had been used. I tried to make that abundantly clear. In addition to that, I have only to say that the whole transaction was based upon the assumption that the rails were not immediately required. I said so very early this afternoon, and that is the reason the government entered into the transaction at all. Because of the fact that the rails were to be used in the future and that the company producing them had to make immediate payments, and inasmuch as it would not be paid for until some time in the future, they would not be reimbursed unless they got the money from the banks for the sums necessarily ex-

pended for production of the rails. The extract read with respect to a portion of the rails referred to the fact that the bank had the security of the raw material, that is, the ore and the limestone, and when the ore and limestone became steel the bank wanted to make it perfectly clear that they did not thereby, in the finished product, lose the lien they had under the Bank Act with respect to the raw material. That is a commonplace with those of us who practise law; it is provided for in the Bank Act itself.
The government has not from day to day asked the extent to which rails have been delivered. I cannot say to-day whether at the Sault they have delivered 2,500 or 2,600 tons, nor where they have delivered them. My colleague from Inverness intimates that delivery has been taken of the whole of the production at Sydney. I was not aware of that fact myself. The extent to which the rails are delivered will of course vary from day to day while delivery is being taken. The hon. member for West Algoma (Mr. Simpson) pointed out that a trainload of some eighty cars of rails had, he understood, gone to the London division. That I estimate would be between 2,500 and 3,000 tons of rails-he informs me that about 4,000 tons have been taken. I suppose the amount changes. I should like to impress once more upon the committee the fact that all that was involved in the transaction was a guarantee to enable the producers of the rails to finance a transaction for which they would not be paid until the future. That is the story.

that perspicuity which is the usual characteristic of fishermen as I know them. Having selected the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough to whom to send the telegram they apparently did not attach much importance it, or they would have sent it to someone who had power to deal with it. I would suggest that it is desirable that they send a telegram either to the Minister of Labour or the Prime Minister or communicate with the premier of their province. I always held in high regard the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough. I have read of Capton Kettle and of the exploits of many of the distinguished figures of fiction and of history, but I have never found anything that excelled the stories I have listened to from the hon. gentleman. But this afternoon he seems to have exceeded anything he ever tried
before, because he has communicated to us that he has been the chosen, the elect of the fishermen themselves to present their claim at the bar of the House of Commons-where there is not one-for the purpose of making known their immediate wants. Now just let me say this: if the province of Nova Scotia will deal with the fishing difficulty exactly as Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba dealt with their difficulties, namely start with the unit, that is with themselves, and from that to the provincial government, and have the provincial government ask the dominion government if they will assist them in discharging this very pleasant avocation, the most serious consideration will be given by this government to every suggestion that may be made in that regard. But that can be done only when we have the power to do it, and at present we have not any such power. Some ten days ago the power lapsed, and until such time as this parliament again confers the power we shall not be able to help the fishermen of Canso either through the government at Halifax or otherwise.
I do not desire to traverse the ground that has been so fully covered on previous occasions as to all these guarantees. I suppose one will have to discuss them many times hereafter and give explanations many, many times, but I think I can summarize all I have to say in a single sentence-

speechtext: Oh, no, no!

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OP RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
I am glad to note that my hon. friend from Lisgar is so pleased to listen to me that he hopes I shall not limit my statement to a single sentence. His anxiety to be instructed is so great and his craving for knowledge so sincere that I shall endeavour to satisfy that want which is always so apparent. May I merely indicate this, that if in the national interest the executive of the day decides to take certain action I do not think it serves any useful purpose to suggest that their motives are improper, because peradventure they have as high a conception of their duty as those who criticize them. If in the discharge of their duties they make mistakes, all people make mistakes, they are fallible; but they exercise their judgment to the best of their ability in the national interest and while they are here they will continue to do so. If the province of Nova Scotia in consequence of representations made to it by the fishermen of Canso request this government to deal with the fishermen of Canso as it dealt with those who required binder twine or seed grain or any other assistance, it will receive exactly
Relief Act, 1934

the same measure of consideration as was dealt out to those others. In the meantime I only hope the hon. gentleman will now give evidence of the faith that is in him by enabling us to get this legislation one step further advanced for that purpose.

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OP RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
I am sure we have listened with interest to the jocular remarks of the Prime Minister on this very important and serious subject concerning the fishermen of Canso, and when the fishermen of Canso read of it in the Halifax papers or in their own paper to-morrow evening they will appreciate the way in which the Prime Minister has handled this question as presented by me. It may be true, of course, that I am an unfortunate medium through which to present this request to the government, but I may say that I received the telegram only to-day. I have not kept it in a pigeon hole; I have not been discourteous even to the government, and it was only after I received the telegram this morning that I realized that I would have an opportunity to-day to lay this matter before not only the Prime Minister, who likes to deal with these big questions himself, and his cabinet, but also before parliament. I consider, sir, that I have done only my plain duty this afternoon in reading this telegram from the mayor of Canso and taking up this matter with the government.
A few moments ago the right hon. gentleman spoke of insulting the intelligence of this committee. Let me say to the right hon. gentleman that he has insulted not only the intelligence of this committee but also my constituents in the town of Canso, and I resent it very much. I may be an unfortunate medium, as I said before, but there are several other unfortunate mediums in this house. I refer to my hon. friend from Cape Breton South. He was unfortunate, of course, in having to come to the Prime Minister to ask for help for his constituents, but from the guarantees which the government gave the different banks in and around Sydney it would seem to be proved conclusively that my right hon. friend the Prime Minister dealt with the matter, so far as the Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation was concerned, from a political point of view, and he is trying to deal with the matter I am bringing up this afternoon in the same way. The same thing applies to the chief whip of the Conservative party, the hon. member for West Algoma; he was also an unfortunate medium, but he had better luck. It may be all right for the Prime Minister to say that this matter should be taken up by the provincial government; let me say that the 
provincial government is doing something already, not directly for the fishermen of Canso but for the fishing industry in the town of Canso. I can say also, without boasting, that in order to help along the fishermen of Canso I purchased 1,200,000 pounds of fish in 1932 which I did not need and almost
1,000,000 pounds in 1933. I did not make a dollar on that fish; I bought it in order to help out the fishermen.

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OP RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext: No guarantee?

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OP RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext: With no guarantee at all, and I got the money from the Bank of Montreal without even an endorsement. Now I say, Mr. Chairman, that in my opinion it is not quite fair for the Prime Minister to say he is going to wait until the provincial government approaches him in connection with this matter. Surely he did not wait for the provincial government to approach him when he gave a guarantee for $60,000,000 in connection with the Canadian Pacific. In a number of other instances he did not wait for the provincial governments to approach him, so why should he wait when I lay this matter before the government, the committee and the house? Therefore I say he is only putting off this matter. It is important to the people in my constituency but it is only a small matter to the government; it amounts only to a guarantee of $15,000, and in my opinion before the snow flies next fall the fishermen of Canso will have paid this money back. My suggestion is that notes be taken for the amount and placed in the Bank of Montreal, and all the government would have to do would be to guarantee that amount.

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OP RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
How about the
fishermen in Nova Scotia generally?

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OP RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
I thought perhaps my hon. friend from Inverness would speak, and I did not want to butt into his territory; I thought he would want to talk about his own fishermen. I thought the hon. member for Cumberland would want to say something, and that the hon. member for Cape Breton South would advocate the condition of his fishermen when he was talking about the steel company. I am sure my hon. friend from Queens-Lunenburg will back me up in what I say, because he was a member of the delegation which waited upon this government two years ago asking for some assistance, which request was turned down. My hon. friend knows the condition of that great fleet which operated out of Lunenburg county ten or fifteen years ago. It is a shame and a disgrace that, because of the lack of a few dollars or a small

Reliej Act, 1934
guarantee a few years ago, this great fleet has been reduced from one hundred and fifty to twenty-five sail. I say this is no time for delay. This is a serious matter. These men want to get to work, to earn some money for their wives and children, and I say to my right hon. friend: Never mind the red tape; cut the red tape, and arrange with the bank that the $15,000 or whatever is necessary may be forthcoming to those fishermen so they may earn their living.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OP RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext: I trust the hon. gentleman knows that this government has no power to give a guarantee. That power lapsed at midnight on March 31.

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OP RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext: That is a quibble.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OP RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext: It is not a quibble, and I ask the hon. gentleman to withdraw that Temark. That is the fact; we have no power to give a guarantee for a five dollar bill.

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OP RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext: You will have, when this bill goes through.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OP RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext: Quite so.

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OP RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext: Will you give a guarantee then, please?

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OP RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OP RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext: I will answer that too. The hon. member for West Lambton very properly pointed out that there has been withdrawn from the bill the power to make guarantees to private enterprises, and no such power is conferred upon this government with respect to any body except a province. When this bill is enacted and the provincial legislature asks for such a guarantee, it may become the subject matter of the terms of an agreement, just as binder twine and seed grain are dealt with in the western provinces. The government does not guarantee seed grain for the farmer, nor does it guarantee him in connection with binder twine, directly. This is what it does: it deals with the province that passes the legislation. The words to which I have referred were taken out of this statute this year because of the criticism offered with respect to them. To-night there is no power in the executive government of Canada to give a guarantee to the Bank of Montreal or any other bank for $15,000 or for any other sum with respect to fishermen or anyone else except through a provincial government.

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OP RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
I have much pleasure in supporting the plea presented by my hon. friend from Antigonish-Guysborough on behalf of those fishermen who have suffered the loss of their gear. In doing so I am heaping
coals of fire upon his head, because I remember the attitude of the Nova Scotians a few days ago when I was pleading for a fair deal for the British Columbia fishermen in the allocation of a certain grant.
The Prime Minister has said, and quite properly, that at the present moment he has no funds and no authority with which to make this grant, but I suggest that he has a place from which he can get the necessary funds;
I refer to the amount of $160,000 already voted for the development of deep sea fisheries in Canada. That is a sum which is voted every year, and it is available now.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OP RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext: Only two-twelfths of that sum is available, and that is for the maritime provinces.

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OP RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
This matter is in the mari-times and the Prime Minister can use the two-twelfths available. While I am not good at mental arithmetic I think two-twelfths of $160,000 would more than provide the amount for which my hon. friend is asking.
I make this further point, because it may be said by hon. members from Nova Scotia that this money should be spent as it has been spent in the past, in miserable little handouts of a dollar a ton to this boat or $2.75 to that fisherman. Several reports have been made in connection with the maritime fishermen; in fact they get altogether too much attention as compared to those in British Columbia. The last report, I think, was made by a firm called Cockfield, Brown and Company, or some such name, and if I remember rightly it cost the government of Canada $10,000, which was about S9,000 more than it was worth. One of the recommendations it contained was that this $160,000 granted annually, which has been frittered away in the manner I have just indicated, as they admitted, should be used in a way more calculated to promote the interests of the fishermen. Here is a case where that money could be profitably used; the Prime Minister says he has not the money and has not the authority to guarantee it, but under that act of 1882 he has the authority, the power and the cash available to-day. By using it in this way he would be doing some real, practical good to the fishermen of Nova Scotia-I am asking for nothing for the fishermen of British Columbia at the moment-instead of having the money frittered away as it has been in the past.

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OP RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext: Thank you.

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OP RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext: Surely he has not laid down this principle-if one may so describe that which he has said to-day-that the member for a constituency has no right to make representations in parliament and to the Prime Minister as to the grievances of his constituents.

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OP RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext: I did not make any such statement.

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OP RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext: I gathered that, most distinctly.

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OP RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext: You usually do gather distinctly, but that is not what I said.

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OP RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext: I did not interrupt my right hon. friend. If I am wrong I am ready to receive any explanation he may wish to make. But I have this impression of what the Prime Minister said in reply to the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough, namely that he was the unfortunate selection-unhappy medium if you like-to represent the views of his constituents.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OP RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext: I did not say that.

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OP RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext: And, if no one else does it, I wish to protest against the idea that any hon. member of this House of Commons cannot make any representation he may wish, at any time, with regard to his constituents. If I have misinterpreted what the Prime Minister said, I should like to have his explanation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OP RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext: Not only does the hon. member entirely misinterpret what I said, but if he will take the trouble to read in Hansard what I said, he will find that what I said I shall be glad to repeat.

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OP RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
I associate myself with
the remarks which have been made by the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough in connection with his request for the fishermen in his constituency. I did not receive any telegram, myself, from the people in my district asking for assistance or support. I, also, may be the unhappy intermediary or medium to lay requests at the door of the government. I do know however that I have had occasion now and then to lay requests before the government for certain public works to be done in my county, and that those requests have on some occasions been turned down

apparently on account of the fact that I was asking for far too much. I feel, as does the hon. member for North Waterloo, that one cannot but be a little apprehensive of the remarks which have been made by the Prime Minister; he left the impression that when hon. members on this side of the house make representations or ask for something from the government they are going to be told that they are unhappy mediums, in a representative capacity, and not the proper people to bring requests to the floor of this parliament from the constituents who elected them to act as their representatives, and to deal with the matters appertaining to their respective counties or districts.
There is another matter I should like to stress. I know that certain requests were to be made to this government and petitions to be signed. Apparently a certain man in my constituency was to be in charge of the patronage, and a petition was sent to him for presentation to the government. I was asked to sign it, and refused to do so for the simple reason, as described by the hon. members for North Waterloo and Antigonish-Guysborough, that the elected member of the House of Commons, whether he be on the opposition side, the government side, or belong to an independent group, is as much a member as is any other member in the house, and is entitled, when he receives a request, to lay it before the government, before hon. members in the house, before the whole country, before any minister of the crown or any other government official.

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OP RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext: And also ask any question he may wish.

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OP RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext: Yes, and ask any question pertaining to a matter before the house. I did not continue the discussion I began this afternoon because I knew some other hon. members wished to speak. I must say, however, that I did not like what the Prime Minister said when I was speaking about the stabilization fund. If I remember correctly he said that I had an ingenious way of delaying matters.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OP RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

We are not. Mr. Chairman, I wish to protest once more against that statement. If we have not the right to put questions, and to exercise our judgment in asking reasons why expenditures have been made and guarantees given, I should like to know why we have not 6uch right. We have asked the Minister of Labour and the Prime Minister for a detailed ex-

Death of Lord Aberdeen
planation as to why the guarantees were given. When we present certain requests to the house we are told that we are the unhappy mediums, and that we are not the proper persons to act between our constituents and the government.
Now, Mr. Chairman, the Prime Minister has said that I was ingenious in delaying matters. Last night we did not delay matters. Who delayed last night? We were ready to vote on the amendment, but at that time the Minister of Labour delayed his own bill, and spoke until eleven o'clock. I say that it is most unfair for hon. members on this side of the house to be told that we are simply delaying matters. The government have made a mess of affairs, even with the powers and authorities with which they have been clothed for the last three years. That fact is brought very forcibly to our notice every time we turn to the estimates.
I suggest that I am entitled, as is the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough and the hon. member for North Waterloo, or in fact any other hon. member, to appear in this chamber and make statements. To-morrow I shall have one or two further questions to ask in connection with these matters, and other hon. members on this side of the house will have questions to put.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OP RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext: There is no doubt about it.

There will be a few
discussions, as there have been to-day. When the bill becomes law we will be able to say to our constituents and to the people at large that we have not shirked our duty, and that we have been able to show where, in the administration of the laws the government has enacted, it has failed.
Progress reported.
